idiom_name: ASP.NET Core versioned endpoint group + Asp.Versioning + generated OpenAPI document
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core supplies the whole publication stack: an endpoint group (MapGroup("/v{version:apiVersion}/orders")) is the host service, the Asp.Versioning packages carry the versioning policy - URL segment, query string, header or media type - and Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi emits the OpenAPI document that consumers and client generators read. DTO records declared next to the endpoints are the translation layer, so entities, aggregates and EF navigation properties never appear in a signature or a response; the classic 'remote facade + DTO' structure is replaced by the framework's endpoint metadata plus a mapper. The framework does not replace the policy decision: without .AddApiVersioning() and an explicit version the current shape silently becomes the contract, and URL-segment versioning hardens into every client's code the moment it ships.
code_sketch:
var v1 = app.NewVersionedApi().MapGroup("/v{version:apiVersion}/orders");
v1.MapPost("/", (SubmitOrder body, IOrderService svc) =>
        Results.Ok(OrderAck.From(svc.Submit(body.ToDomain()))))  // DTOs only
  .MapToApiVersion(1.0)
  .WithOpenApi();                                                 // published document
pitfalls: Serialising EF entities puts persistence annotations, navigation properties and internal ids on the wire - always return records you own.
Choosing URL-segment versioning bakes the version into every route; decide URL vs header vs media type before the first consumer integrates, because switching later breaks all of them.
Without AddApiVersioning()/ApiVersion metadata the OpenAPI document shows one unversioned shape while the code serves several - consumers cannot tell which contract they are coding against.
